analysis.investment_thesis: Dr. Agarwal's is a legitimate fast-grower story — 26.4% revenue CAGR in a structurally underpenetrated Indian eye-care market — but at P/E 110x with stagnating net profits (₹103 Cr → ₹95 Cr → ₹110 Cr over three years), you're paying a decade's worth of growth upfront. The PEG ratio of ~3x (P/E 110 / ~30% growth) is three times my ceiling of 1.0; the story is good, the price is ruinous.
key_strengths: Revenue growing 26.4% CAGR (2020→2025) in structurally underpenetrated Indian eye-care market — a 'story' anyone can observe walking into any tier-2 city.
OCF consistently positive all 5 years, reaching ₹360 Cr in FY25 — the core operating engine does generate cash.
Hospital roll-up with rising EBITDA (17.7% CAGR) and strong gross margin (42.6%) shows pricing power at the procedure level.
key_risks: PEG ratio ~3–4x: P/E 110 divided by even an optimistic 30% earnings growth rate = 3.7x — Lynch's hard ceiling is 1.0; this is disqualifying.
Net profit growth has stalled and is barely growing: ₹43 Cr (FY22) → ₹103 Cr (FY23) → ₹95 Cr (FY24) → ₹110 Cr (FY25); capital-intensive expansion is not converting to earnings.
FCF collapsed to ₹40 Cr in FY25 on ₹321 Cr capex and ₹115 Cr finance costs — the expansion is devouring cash; ROE of 4.76% is well below any reasonable cost of equity.
red_flags: PEG ratio 3.5–4x — the single most disqualifying metric for a Lynch-style investment.
ROE 4.76% is value-destructive at current market valuation and debt levels.
Promoter holding only 32.35% — low skin in the game for a company executing a high-stakes capex rollout.
Free cash flow has DECLINED from ₹118 Cr (FY24) to ₹40 Cr (FY25) even as revenue surged — the unit economics of new hospitals are dilutive.
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Dr. Agarwal's passes the 'story' test with flying colors — eye care in India is chronically underpenetrated, the aging population theme is real, and I can see the hospitals proliferating in every city. Revenue has compounded at 26.4% and EBITDA at 17.7% over five years, which shows the core franchise is growing. But Lynch's rule is that you don't just find a good story — you find a good story at a price that hasn't already discounted the next decade. At P/E 110x on ₹110 Cr of net profit against a ₹14,075 Cr market cap, this stock has already priced in perfection and then some. The forward P/E of 77x assumes dramatic profit acceleration that the last three years of near-flat net earnings give no reason to expect.

The deeper structural problem is the capital intensity. Investing outflows have ballooned from ₹509 Cr (FY23) to ₹914 Cr (FY24) to ₹750 Cr (FY25), funded by equity raises and debt (borrowings now ₹983 Cr, finance costs ₹115 Cr/year). Each new hospital takes years to mature, keeping ROE pinned at a dismal 4.76% and ROCE barely below 10%. A hospital roll-up that can't generate returns above its cost of capital is not a fast-grower — it's a slow compounding of dilution. I'd love to revisit this at P/E 40–50x with net profits clearly inflecting above ₹200 Cr and FCF recovering, but today's price demands a flawless execution I can't see in the numbers.
